reasoning:
Both submissions make the SAME single functional change: in clrCastleSq's a1 branch (cp 0x00), the mask 0xFE becomes 0xFD. Everything else in either diff is comment text; the emitted Z80 bytes are byte-for-byte identical between X and Y. So they are genuinely equivalent on correctness and can only be separated on scope and legibility.

Correctness (both 5). With castling = bit0 WK, bit1 WQ, bit2 BK, bit3 BQ, `and 0xFE` on the a1 corner clears bit0 — the KINGSIDE right — which is the h1 mask misapplied to a1. That one wrong operand accounts for every reported symptom: repro 3 (e1-g1 refused after a1a2, because the kingside bit was the one revoked), repro 2 (e1-c1 still accepted with the a1 rook standing on a2, because the queenside bit was never cleared), the Kiwipete-only perft mismatch on a position that starts with all four rights while perft 1-4 from the initial position pass, and the h1/a8/h8 corners behaving correctly. The phantom rook and Matl 5→10 at the turn boundary follow from the same retained-but-unbacked queenside right: the engine keeps a right for a corner whose rook has left, and the state gets reconciled back onto the board on the opponent's move. The control case in the report supports this reading — h1h2 correctly refuses O-O and produces no phantom rook on h1, i.e. exactly the corner whose mask is right. `and 0xFD` (11111101) clears bit1 alone and preserves bit0, which is precisely "revoke queenside and nothing else"; it cannot affect the black corners or any non-corner square, since it lives inside the `cp 0x00 / jr nz,cc1` branch. Neither submission touches control flow, register usage, or the routine's A/B contract, so neither carries regression risk beyond the intended behaviour change. I found no residual defect either fix leaves behind; the only thing neither does in code is validate the a8/h8 masks, and X at least asserts them in prose.

Minimality. Y is the tighter diff: 13 lines in, 13 out, one operand changed plus two same-line comments. 5. X spends five extra lines on a header comment. That is still tightly scoped — comment-only, at the fault site, no code motion — but it is measurably more than the defect strictly requires, so 4. I deliberately did not treat the longer diff as better by default; on this axis alone Y wins.

Clarity. X is stronger: it states the routine's contract ("a rook leaving (or being captured on) a corner kills THAT corner's right and only that one"), cites the source of truth for the bitfield (chess.asm:39), and tabulates all four corner masks — a1 0xFD, h1 0xFE, a8 0xF7, h8 0xFB. Those values are internally consistent with the stated layout (a8 is black QUEENSIDE → clear bit3 → 0xF7; h8 → bit2 → 0xFB) and consistent with the report's finding that the other three corners already behave correctly, so a reviewer can verify every branch of the dispatch without opening another file. X also flags the changed line inline. 5. Y's two comments are accurate and do name the bits, so a reviewer can check 0xFD against "bit 1" and 0xFE against "bit 0" — genuinely helpful — but they cover only two of four branches and give no layout reference, leaving the a8/h8 constants below as unannotated magic numbers. 4.

Merge: X, narrowly. Since the runtime change is identical, the tiebreak is which version better protects against a recurrence, and the bug here WAS a mis-transcribed entry in a four-row mask table. X documents that table in full at the exact site, making the fix self-checking; Y annotates half of it. X's extra scope is comments only, so it buys that for no correctness cost. Y would be a perfectly acceptable merge too, and if the project's house rule is minimum-diff, Y is the defensible pick — the gap is small and is about durability, not about the repair itself.

Blinding note: X's file:line citation and fuller documentation discipline did prompt a passing theory about differing authoring processes; I set that aside and scored only the shown assembly and comments, which is why both submissions carry the same correctness score rather than being split on style-derived assumptions.
